### Description

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/671fe42d8a5eb90556d60238cfdf28c0753fdae1/src/libraries/System.Text.RegularExpressions/tests/FunctionalTests/UpgradeToRegexGeneratorAnalyzerTests.cs#L48

None of the constructors has a "timeout" parameter. I believe the test wanted to refer to this constructor, but the parameter was misspelled. I'm not sure though if the lack of `options` parameter is an intentional error scenario to test.

```csharp

```

@joperezr What was the intention here?

I discovered this while enabling validation of compiler diagnostics in tests.

review_comments: Can you explain why we are not using Diagnostics nor validating that they match what is thrown any longer?
@joperezr The `[|code|]` syntax does the exact same thing. It asserts the analyzer produces a diagnostic that squiggle `code`.

This looks a bit fishy, we used to have a way where we would only verify that an analyzer would throw some diagnostics, and one way to validate a codefix was produced, but now all analyzer calls will also validate the CodeFix produced the same exact source?

@joperezr 

There are two cases:

1. `source` doesn't have any diagnostics, in this case both approaches are exactly the same
2. `source` has diagnostics, in this case the new approach is more strict. The difference is:
    - previously we will verify the diagnostics.
    - Now we will verify the diagnostic, and verify that *no codefix is offered*.

The use of `VerifyCodeFixAsync(source, source)` is actually a very common pattern in both dotnet/roslyn and dotnet/roslyn-analyzers.

Oh I understand now, so this method is effectively not used now when we expect a diagnostic, instead we are now only using it when we expect no diagnostics to be thrown right? In such case, I would just rename from `VerifyAnalyzerAsync` to something like `VerifyNoDiagnosticsThrown`

Technically, the method can be used to verify a diagnostic that has no codefix.

Currently, the codefix is capable of fixing any analyzer diagnostics, but in future, you might find cases where the analyzer reports a diagnostic that the codefix isn't capable of handling.

Just as an example, we could decide to report diagnostics in top-level, but not offer a fix (this is not true today definitely, just an example). If that happened, then this method asserts we don't offer a codefix, rather than offering a codefix that does "nothing".

By does "nothing", I mean we register the codefix (ie, it appears in lightbulb), but we immediately return the original document (selecting the code action from lightbulb will have no effect).
